name: Alcubierre Warp Drive
description: A warp bubble metric that contracts space ahead of a ship and expands it behind, allowing travel that is effectively faster than light without locally exceeding light speed. It requires negative energy density (exotic matter) to sustain the bubble.
history: The warp drive is the rare exact solution that began as a piece of science fiction taken seriously. In 1994 Miguel Alcubierre, then in Wales, asked whether Star Trek's travel faster than light could be given an honest general relativistic description, and found that it could [alcubierre1994]. His construction places the ship in a flat bubble of spacetime and contracts space ahead of the bubble while expanding it behind. Stephen Baxter carried the metric back into science fiction the next year: in his story "Gossamer" the collapsing mouth of a wormhole throws off an Alcubierre wave, a moment of negative energy that distorts a chunk of spacetime and carries two travellers superluminally down to Pluto [baxter1995gossamer]. André Bormanis, producer and science consultant of Seth MacFarlane's series The Orville, which began on Fox in 2017, explains the quantum drive of its ship through Alcubierre's space expanding behind and contracting ahead [macfarlane2017orville, bormanis2017quantum].¶Locally nothing moves faster than light, since the ship sits at rest in its own little patch, yet the bubble itself glides through spacetime at any speed one likes. Special relativity forbids outrunning a light beam locally; it says nothing about how fast a region of space may be made to move. The difficulty is the source: to bend spacetime this way the Einstein equations demand a region of negative energy density, exotic matter that violates the energy conditions every known form of matter obeys.¶The negative energy needed is enormous. In 1997 Michael Pfenning and Lawrence Ford applied quantum inequalities to the bubble and found that its walls must be only a few hundred Planck lengths thick, and that the total negative energy required exceeds, by many orders of magnitude, anything physically conceivable, comparable in scale to all the mass and energy of the visible universe [pfenning1997]. The warp drive therefore remains a thought experiment, though a remarkably productive one.¶The drive sharpened the question of how far the energy conditions can be pushed, and it spawned a family of variants. In 1999 Chris Van Den Broeck showed that a clever change of the bubble's shape, a tiny throat opening into a large interior, could cut the required negative energy from the scale of a universe down to a few solar masses [vandenbroeck1999]. José Natário showed in 2002 that the ship needs no contraction ahead and expansion behind, constructing a warp drive with no volume expansion [natario2002]. The central obstruction held: in 2004 Francisco Lobo and Matt Visser showed that the energy conditions fail for bubbles of every speed, however slow [lobo2004].¶Alexey Bobrick, Gianni Martire, and Erik Lentz took up the question of the source again in 2021. Bobrick and Martire gave a general framework that encompasses every warp drive metric yet proposed and clarified which of their features are negotiable, describing physical, subluminal warp drives free of the worst pathologies [bobrick2021]; Lentz exhibited soliton solutions that can in principle be sourced by purely positive energy densities drawn from a conducting plasma and classical electromagnetic fields, the first warp geometries built from familiar matter [lentz2021]. Whether anyone could build such a drive remains open. General relativity permits the geometry, and the energy conditions mark where it resists.

related.text: Warp drives with any shift vector $(u, v, w)$. José Natário found one in 2002 that neither expands nor contracts space anywhere [natario2002].

Alcubierre's bubble with a factor $B^2$ on its space, which hides a pocket 200 m across inside a bubble a few femtometres wide. That brings the negative energy down to a few solar masses [vandenbroeck1999].

A warp drive whose shift is the gradient of a potential, which Erik Lentz built in 2021 to have positive energy density for the observers riding with it [lentz2021]. Other observers still measure negative energy [santiago2022].

A second way to beat light with negative energy. A pilot inside an Alcubierre bubble cannot reach its wall to steer it, and Krasnikov's tube is laid down by a ship moving slower than light [krasnikov1998, everett1997].

The other way to cross space faster than light could in flat spacetime, a tunnel where Alcubierre has a bubble. Alcubierre set his drive beside it: "just as it happens with wormholes, exotic matter will be needed" [alcubierre1994].

A wormhole turned into a time machine by moving one of its mouths. Allen Everett showed in 1996 that a simple change to Alcubierre's bubble allows causal loops as well, as Alcubierre had conjectured [everett1996].
The drive switched off. With $v_s = 0$ the metric is Minkowski's, and with the bubble moving spacetime is still flat inside it and far from it [alcubierre1994].

A bubble built on Alcubierre's recipe whose path closes on itself in spacetime. Benjamin Tippett and David Tsang sent it round a circle in the plane of $t$ and $x$ in 2017, and a rider who keeps accelerating inside it meets her own past [tippett2017].

parameters.description: Bubble velocity in units of $c$, an arbitrary function of $t$ alone. The centre of the bubble follows the world line $x = x_s(t)$ with $dx_s/dt = c\,v_s(t)$, and nothing in the solution bounds it, so $v_s > 1$ is allowed and is the whole point of the construction: the ship rides at rest in its own flat patch and no local measurement ever catches it outrunning a light ray. The prime is the derivative along the chart coordinate, $v_s' = dv_s/d(ct)$, so it carries an inverse length.

Shape function, dimensionless, an arbitrary function of the four coordinates. It is $1$ at the centre of the bubble and $0$ far outside it, and the wall is wherever it falls between, so every derivative of $f$ is supported on the wall alone and the spacetime is flat everywhere else. Alcubierre's own choice is the radial profile $f(r_s)$ built from hyperbolic tangents, with $r_s = \sqrt{(x - x_s(t))^2 + y^2 + z^2}$ the distance from the centre of the bubble, but no component needs it. A profile that depends on $t$ and $x$ only through $x - x_s(t)$ obeys $\partial_t f = -v_s\,\partial_x f$ in this chart, and that is the one relation the components are not allowed to assume, since they are identities for an arbitrary $f$.

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ lengths. The velocity $v_s$ of the bubble is in units of $c$, so its centre follows $x = x_s(t)$ with $dx_s/dt = c\,v_s$, and the shape function $f$ is a dimensionless function of all four coordinates. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, where $\partial_t = c^{-1}\partial/\partial t$ and $v_s' = dv_s/d(ct)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
